# Is the helicopter on the ground?

## Short answer

**Yes — I can tell, and the helicopter is on the ground.** For the whole portion of
the clip I was able to examine, the aircraft is sitting on a rocky, gravel-covered
high-desert slope with its main rotor turning at speed. It is running, but it is
not flying — neither in forward flight nor in a hover.

## What the clip actually is

The file is a 360°/VR capture: 3072x1536 (2:1 equirectangular), 24 fps, nominally
120.7 s long. One caveat up front, stated plainly: **the file on disk is
truncated.** It is only ~10.7 MB against a ~9.5 Mbit/s bitrate, so only the first
~8 seconds (190 frames) actually decode; everything after that is a corrupt or
missing packet. All of the analysis below therefore comes from that opening
~8-second window.

The aircraft is a UH-60 Black Hawk. Two pilots are in the cockpit, at least one
more crew member sits at the cabin window, and camouflage-covered gear is stowed
loose on the cabin floor. A burned-in title reads "360° — Colorado Army National
Guard — High-Altitude ARNG Aviation Training Site" (HAATS). The 360 camera is
clamped low on the airframe on the left side, so a single frame simultaneously
shows the cabin interior, a main rotor blade, the surrounding terrain, and the
ground immediately beneath the aircraft.

## The evidence that it is on the ground

**1. The ground below the aircraft does not move at all — across 8 full seconds.**
This is the single strongest piece of evidence. I compared the patch of ground
directly beneath the airframe at frame 0, frame 95 (~4 s) and frame 190 (~7.9 s),
at native resolution. Individual gravel stones, a pale rectangular object lying on
the surface, and a juniper bush sit on *exactly* the same pixels in all three
frames. A difference image of frame 0 against frame 190 is essentially blank across
the entire ground area. No aircraft in flight produces that: forward flight would
replace the scene entirely, and even a very well held hover drifts and yaws
visibly over eight seconds.

**2. Motion estimation puts a number on it.** Running a motion-vector analysis over
a 1400x400 px window of the ground, the per-frame local displacements are
overwhelmingly 0 to 2 pixels, with mixed signs and no consistent direction — pure
vibration, with essentially zero accumulated translation over the 190 frames. The
only large outlier vectors come from the two genuinely moving things in that
window: the camera mount and a sweeping shadow (see below).

**3. What does move is the airframe, not the world.** In the same comparisons the
camera's clamp mount and the lower edge of the fuselage/door sill jitter by a few
pixels, and the fuselage edge sits at a slightly different height at frame 190 than
at frame 0. So the airframe is shaking while the ground stays nailed in place.
That is the signature of a helicopter standing on its landing gear with the rotor
turning — the body rocks a little on the oleo struts while the wheels stay planted.
If the aircraft were airborne the relationship would be inverted: the airframe
would be the steady reference and the ground would be the thing sliding.

**4. The rotor is definitely turning, so it is running rather than shut down.**
Stepping through consecutive frames, the main rotor blade — identifiable by its
orange-painted tip cap — sweeps a large angle every 1/24 s frame, consistent with
normal operating RPM. The correct description is therefore *on the ground with
rotors turning*, which is also why the shot still has a "flying" feel to it.

**5. Rotor blade shadows sweep across the ground right next to the aircraft.**
Tiling a patch of nearby gravel across frames 0, 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 shows a soft,
elongated dark band sweeping across the surface and off the edge of the patch,
repeating at a rate consistent with blade passage aliased against the 24 fps
sampling. The shadows are soft-edged, as you would expect from a rotor disc a few
metres above the surface. The rotor disc is therefore casting onto terrain that is
right there beside the aircraft.

**6. There is no downwash signature on the surroundings.** The air is completely
clear — no dust, no haze, no debris in motion — over dry, loose, decomposed-granite
gravel that would be trivially easy to blow around. The juniper bush a few metres
off the aircraft is absolutely motionless across all 190 frames and casts a sharp,
unblurred shadow. A Black Hawk hovering over that surface would throw up an obvious
dust cloud and thrash that vegetation. On the ground with the collective flat,
downwash is minimal — which is exactly what we see.

**7. The ground is very close and sharply resolved.** Looking down from the camera,
individual angular gravel chips a few centimetres across are clearly resolved right
beneath the fuselage and door sill, along with a small pale rectangular object and
scuffed patches of dirt. Terrain that close and that sharply detailed puts the
camera on the order of a metre or two above the surface, not airborne.

**8. Shadows sit right against the aircraft.** The shadow cast by the aircraft's
lower structure falls on the gravel immediately below it, rather than being
displaced away across the terrain as it would be if the machine were standing off
the ground.

**9. The surrounding terrain is at cabin level, not below it.** Through the cockpit
windscreen and the cabin windows you see close-up rocky ground, scrub and a dirt
track at roughly the level of the cabin and slightly above it, with the slope then
falling away to a valley and distant mountain ranges. Looking out the right-side
cabin windows, the frames are filled entirely with near ground — no sky, no
horizon. The surface runs continuously from directly underneath the aircraft out to
the horizon with no break. That is the view from a machine parked on a
hillside/ridge, not one looking down at terrain from altitude.

**10. Crew posture is consistent with being on the ground.** The pilots are seated
normally, gear is loose on the cabin floor, and nobody is braced. Weak evidence on
its own, but consistent with everything else.

## Limits on this conclusion

- Only the first ~8 seconds of the 121-second clip are recoverable from the file,
  so what I can state confidently is that the aircraft is on the ground **during
  that window**. Given that the rotor is at operating speed, it is entirely
  plausible that the aircraft lifts off later in the full clip — I simply cannot
  see that footage.
- I could not get a direct, unambiguous view of a main wheel touching the dirt. The
  metallic hardware visible near the bottom of the panorama, which looks at first
  glance like a landing gear strut, is actually the 360 camera's own clamp mount,
  with the out-of-focus dark lobes of the mount/camera body occluding the nadir.
  Ground contact is therefore inferred from the zero relative motion, the absence of
  downwash, the closeness of the surface and the attached shadows, rather than seen
  as a wheel-on-dirt contact patch.
- Any single still frame here would be genuinely ambiguous — the geometry alone
  could pass for a low hover. It is the *temporal* evidence — 190 consecutive frames
  with zero ground drift and zero dust — that makes the call solid.
